detail.abstract_excerpt: I tested 25 of the most popular package managers to check whether they detect a compromised package repository injecting malicious code into legitimate packages. This code integrity problem could be solved using cryptographic hashes or signatures, but many package managers are still vulnerable to this threat. Of the 25 package managers reviewed 1 , fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded. Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits 2 , are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table. Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below. Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures. Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats. As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future. Simulating malicious package repositories Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server. Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another. The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package. uuid : dependency : "direct main" description : name : uuid sha256 : "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd" url : "https://pub.dev" source : hosted version : "4.6.0" If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated. This is documented behavior , and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation 6 . Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected. Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++. "requires" : [ "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337" ] , This includes the package name ( zlib ), the version number ( 1.3.1 ), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20 , and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository. "source" : { "git" : "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git" , "tag" : "4.0.2" } , So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag. Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt. "dist" : { "type" : "zip" , "url" : "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "reference" : "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "shasum" : "" } , However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer. Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. This post focuses on dependency managers for source code rather than system package managers like APT, Chocolatey, or Homebrew. The line between the two is blurred, but concentrating on one helps highlight particular usage and deployment patterns in that group. ↩︎ Trail of Bits has several ongoing and completed projects to improve supply-chain security in some of these package ecosystems, including helping address both account takeover threats and the cryptographic integrity problem. ↩︎ cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl , but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎ A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎ Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎ Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test , call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub . ↩︎ The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. The latter supports signatures, and the server protocol is implemented by private services such as JFrog Artifactory and AWS CodeArtifact . As far as I can find, there is no repository for the general public that implements this protocol, so I tested the signatureless Git format. ↩︎ Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎ Although I did not test PowerShell on Windows, the documented default ExecutionPolicy behavior is to block scripts on Windows client machines, and to require a valid signature for Windows servers. This achieves package integrity. ↩︎ Go calls these downloadable artifacts “modules,” which consist of “packages.” For the sake of consistent terminology with the rest of the post, I use “package” in the general sense, not the Go-specific one. ↩︎ The go.sum file stores hashes, but it is not a lockfile . Instead, it is a local cache for entries from the checksum database. ↩︎

detail.abstract_excerpt: In much of the distributed computing literature, latency is expressed as the number of communication rounds or network delays; such metrics do not directly account for the amount of data sent or the dependencies among parties sending the data. Throughput is also normally evaluated empirically. As a consequence, the standard models used for analysing state machine replication (SMR) protocols do not by themselves provide an end-to-end analytical comparison of practical latency and throughput as functions of per-processor bandwidth and transaction arrival rate. In this paper, we present Pipes, a model for analysing latency and throughput in SMR protocols. The Pipes model captures the effect of processor bandwidth $S$, transaction arrival rate $D$, and network delays, enabling us to explicitly specify the throughput bottleneck and the latency of a protocol. Using Pipes, we derive good-case latency expressions and throughput bottlenecks for concrete multi-shot protocols implementing Best-effort Broadcast, Consistent Broadcast, Reliable Broadcast, and Reliable Broadcast with erasure coding and pipelining. We consider both single-sender and multi-sender approaches, and extend the analysis to SMR protocols including DispersedSimplex, Sailfish, Tendermint, and HotStuff. Our comparisons reveal the trade-off between the lower latency achievable through pipelining and erasure coding in single-sender protocols and the higher throughput bottlenecks achievable by multi-sender DAG-based protocols. We also quantify when the additional communication phases of HotStuff are preferable to the fixed wait in a Tendermint-style protocol. Beyond these protocol-specific latency calculations, we establish tight Best-effort Broadcast latency bounds in both the single-sender and multi-sender settings. The analysed protocols are optimal when each recipient receives a full block directly from the transaction's source, the same blocks are sent to everyone, and outstanding upload work is bounded. We give a second tight bound assuming only direct receipt, attained by a protocol that staggers block boundaries across recipients. For protocols using AVID-style erasure coding, we prove latency lower bounds that combine block formation, reconstruction and fragment forwarding. Finally, we implement and evaluate variants of DispersedSimplex and Sailfish, comparing measured latency with the predictions of the Pipes model.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Pseudorandom error-correcting codes (PRCs), introduced by Christ and Gunn at CRYPTO’24, combine pseudorandomness with error correction, providing a natural abstraction for robust watermarking and steganography on generative AI models. Subsequent standalone notions, which are ideal security for secret-key PRCs and CCA-style security for public-key PRCs, are oracle-based and do not capture composable use with explicit parties, sessions, and corruption. We give a UC treatment of PRCs via corruption-aware ideal functionalities for both settings. Under non-adaptive corruption, the UC notions recover the standalone ones. Under adaptive corruption, we identify a common obstruction: dummy codewords sampled before corruption, together with their neighborhoods, must later be opened as valid PRC codewords. We formalize this as a decoder-non-committing code (NC-PRC), which any adaptively UC-secure realization must induce. We then capture failures of such openings via targeted low opening capacity, show it rules out robust NC-PRCs, and prove that LDPC-based PRCs have this property hence do not admit a NC-PRC. On the positive side, we sketch two heuristic compilers to lift error-correcting codes to admit NC-PRCs: a secret-key one from a puncturable PRF and indistinguishability obfuscation (iO), and a public-key one from a smooth projective hash function (SPHF), both evading the barrier via programmable acceptance. Finally, we identify a fresh-codeword explanation barrier for public-key PRCs: accepted unseen codewords cannot be explained from public information without violating pseudorandomness, hence public-key UC realizations require a trapdoor or an idealized setup, and PRC-based watermark detection is inherently designated-verifier.

detail.abstract_excerpt: BitVM-style protocols verify succinct proofs on Bitcoin by garbling a proof veriﬁer oﬀ-chain. What reaches the chain in a dispute is the proof itself: its bits under one-time keys, the scripts that authenticate them and the signatures that bind them to transactions. Existing designs garble elliptic-curve succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge (SNARK) veriﬁers, which a quantum adversary breaks. Our goal is a post-quantum alternative: a hash-based scalable transparent argument of knowledge (STARK) veriﬁer, garbled and fed with hash-based one-time keys, with no number-theoretic assumption anywhere in the veriﬁer; its price is a far larger proof, and this paper measures and reduces that on-chain data. We compile the complete veriﬁer for WHIR-based STARK proofs from Ziren into a Boolean circuit using free-XOR gadgets for binary-tower arithmetic and Blake3. Our implementation uses Ziren’s binary-ﬁeld proof stage and narrow recursion. For an Ethereum block proved through four recursion levels, the ﬁnal recursive WHIR-proof veriﬁer has 175.4M non-free gates and 520,832 input bits, corresponding to 2.81 GB of garbled tables, and publishing that input with translated Winternitz keys takes 3.93 million virtual bytes (MvB), in 41 standard transactions. The costs are coupled: on-chain cost grows linearly with the input bits, oﬀ-chain storage with the gate count, and proving time exponentially with the grinding that shortens the input. The WHIR schedule, the Merkle cap depth and the input encoding trade these costs against one another, and a model of proof size and proving time selects the setting, a step toward practical post-quantum Bitcoin bridges.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The shuffle model is a widely used abstraction for non-interactive anonymous communication. It allows $n$ parties holding private inputs $x_1,\dots,x_n$ to simultaneously send messages to an evaluator, so that the messages are received in a random order. The evaluator can then compute a joint function $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, ideally while learning nothing else about the private inputs. The model has become increasingly popular both in cryptography, as an alternative to non-interactive secure computation in trusted setup models, and even more so in differential privacy, as an intermediate between the high-privacy, little-utility local model and the little-privacy, high-utility central curator model. The main open question in this context is which functions $f$ can be computed in the shuffle model with statistical security. While general feasibility results were obtained using public-key cryptography, the question of statistical security has remained elusive. The common conjecture has been that even relatively simple functions cannot be computed with statistical security in the shuffle model. We refute this conjecture, showing that all functions can be computed in the shuffle model with statistical security. In particular, any differentially private mechanism in the central curator model can also be realized in the shuffle model with essentially the same utility, and while the evaluator learns nothing beyond the central model result. This feasibility result is obtained by constructing a statistically secure additive randomized encoding (ARE) for any function. An ARE randomly maps individual inputs to group elements whose sum only reveals the function output. Similarly to other types of randomized encoding of functions, our statistical ARE is efficient for functions in $NC^1$ or $NL$. Alternatively, we get computationally secure ARE for all polynomial-time functions using a one-way function. More generally, we can convert any (information-theoretic or computational) ``garbling scheme'' to an ARE with a constant-factor size overhead.

Choosing $c>1$ gives a hash function which can be implemented using $c$-way single instruction multiple data (SIMD) instructions. We report a set of very comprehensive hand optimised assembly implementations of 4-decBRWHash using avx2 SIMD instructions available on modern Intel processors. detail.abstract_excerpt: Integral distinguishers can reveal more than a zero-sum property: the number of ones in an output component may be divisible by a high power of $2$, rather than merely being even. To exploit this divisibility, we relate linear, integral, differential-linear, and restricted differential sums through two-way conversions with explicit divisibility guarantees and data complexity, recovering established links as special cases. We derive exact random-permutation probabilities and rigorous bounds to quantify the distinguishing strength while accounting for dependencies between output conditions. To discover these properties, we develop automated MILP/SAT models that use complete-round Walsh coefficients or combine Walsh and ultrametric representations to obtain stronger bounds. These weighted models prove finite divisibility even when compatible trails exist, beyond what trail-existence tests alone can establish. For differential-linear sums, we show that combining differential and linear propagation with local zeros in a differential-linear connectivity table (DLCT) can give false zero-correlation claims. We address this limitation with exact mix-basis models that establish zero correlation and finite divisibility. To complement these symbolic methods, we provide a black-box algorithm using exact histograms and the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform to search all output masks for selected input conditions and identify zeros and finite divisibility properties. Our MILP/SAT models significantly improve the divisibility bounds reported by Beyne and Verbauwhede in 674 cases across the SIMON family, as well as for PRESENT, without trail enumeration and at unchanged data complexity. For example, we raise the bounds from $2^5$ to $2^{11}$ on 9-round SIMON32 and from $2^6$ to $2^{22}$ on 10-round SIMON48. To our knowledge, we are the first to prove higher divisibility for 8-round SPECK and for BEANIE, with new bounds for GIFT-64 and Ascon and exact counts for SKINNY-64. Our black-box searches reveal new properties on RC5, ChiLow-32, KeeLoq, and KATAN32, including output-bit combinations missed by single-bit searches, and lead us to introduce probabilistic divisibility: conditions that hold more often than for a random permutation.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Taxes are harder to enforce on the self-employed than on wage earners, creating horizontal inequities among taxpayers with similar incomes. Using tax microsimulation and household survey data from 29 developing countries, we show that horizontal inequities in actual tax systems are comparable in magnitude to vertical equity and are exacerbated by progressive reforms that fall disproportionately on wage earners. We then conduct surveys and randomized information experiments in Pakistan to study public perceptions of these inequities. Although providing information raises fairness concerns, it does not increase support for reforms reducing it, revealing an important political constraint to improving tax equity.

These inflationary effects can be significant in relevant ranges of interest rates; they exist in the short run even when interest rate hikes succeed in cutting aggregate demand; and that they are amplified by policy uncertainty and the uncertainty about the effects of interest rate changes, both of which have increased as conventional policy has demonstrably failed badly to keep inflation at the 2% target. Empirical studies confirm this low level of ineffectiveness of raising interest rates in reducing inflation. The weakening effectiveness of monetary policy was predicted by our earlier work on banks and the supply of credit, as a result of the elimination of interest prohibition on deposits; and further suggested by work on the structural transformation of the economy, as customer markets become more important.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Summary Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.

detail.abstract_excerpt: Science is producing knowledge at unprecedented scale, while artificial intelligence promises to accelerate the generation of hypotheses, analyses, and scientific outputs further. Yet increasing the volume of research does not necessarily expand the range of directions science effectively explores. We argue that science can be understood as a collective search process in which finite resources are allocated across an evolving space of possible research trajectories. Careers, funding, organization, publication, attention, and technology act as interacting selection mechanisms that shape this allocation. This Perspective distinguishes the visible diversity of scientific activity from its effective diversity: apparently different researchers, institutions, or projects need not provide genuinely different routes of exploration or evaluation. Our principal contribution is to introduce cross-stage dependence, which occurs when selection processes operating at different stages of science are not fully independent in the grounds through which they favour scientific trajectories. We hypothesize that, under uncertainty, repeated filtering through overlapping criteria, information, prior selections, or technological infrastructure can reduce the capacity of science to maintain plausible alternatives and redirect effort when evidence changes their relative promise. Artificial intelligence makes this problem increasingly consequential because it can simultaneously expand scientific search capacity and participate across multiple stages of production and selection. The challenge is therefore not simply to produce more knowledge, but to preserve sufficiently distinct routes of exploration, verification and correction while retaining the ability to change direction.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The complexity of games is a central topic in combinatorics, algorithms, and computational complexity theory. It asks how difficult it is to determine the winner of a combinatorial game under optimal play. Many games, such as Hex or Othello, are PSPACE-complete: the game tree has polynomial depth, so the game can be decided in PSPACE. However, some games allow exponentially long plays, for instance Chess (without a generalized 50-move rule) or Go under Japanese rules; these are complete for exponential time. To prevent infinite games, some games employ a no-repetition rule (super-ko rule), for instance Go under Chinese rules. Robson (1984) proved that Chess and Checkers with a no-repetition rule are even harder: deciding whether the first player has a winning strategy is EXPSPACE-complete. Since then, it has been an open problem whether Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete, too. The complexity of a game under a no-repetition rule is typically interpreted as follows: given a board position, decide whether the first player has a winning strategy such that no repetition occurs from that position on. We introduce the concept of a succinct game history: a Boolean circuit that, given a board position, outputs 1 if the position is in the game history and 0 otherwise. It serves as a "judge" that tells the players whether a move is illegal because it creates a repetition. We prove that deciding whether Black has a winning strategy in Go with a no-repetition rule is EXPSPACE-complete when the game history is given succinctly. Moreover, the starting position in our hardness proof is reachable by legal gameplay, which has not always been the case in prior proofs.

detail.abstract_excerpt: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.

For instance, architectures such as the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) have been trained on numerical datasets generated by isolated, stiff ionic models to provide a data-driven alternative to traditional numerical integration schemes. Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed approach on empirical data, demonstrating its ability to accurately and efficiently model task-oriented neural activity.

detail.abstract_excerpt: The tournament equilibrium set (TEQ), proposed by Schwartz in 1990, is a classical voting rule based on pairwise majority comparisons. Its definition is recursive: an alternative is judged by the alternatives that beat it, called its dominators, and by which of those dominators TEQ itself selects. Deciding whether a given alternative belongs to TEQ was known to be NP-hard and to lie in PSPACE. We close this gap by proving that the problem is PSPACE-complete. To our knowledge, this is the first PSPACE-completeness result for membership in a tournament solution. The hardness persists even when every nonempty subtournament has a unique minimal retentive set, the property conjectured by Schwartz to hold for all tournaments. Moreover, every such subtournament in our hard instances contains an alternative with at most three dominators. We prove that a single alternative with at most four dominators suffices both to guarantee uniqueness and to find a TEQ winner in $O(N^2)$ time. Thus, on our hard instances, finding one winner is efficient even though recognizing a specified winner is PSPACE-complete. We also study how the complexity changes with the dominator bound. If every nonempty subtournament has an alternative with at most one dominator, the entire TEQ can be computed in quadratic time; allowing two dominators makes membership NP-hard. Under the same condition with four dominators, all $t$ winners can be computed in $O(2^t N^2)$ time, where $N$ is the number of alternatives.

detail.abstract_excerpt: In the submodular secretary problem with a cardinality constraint, $n$ elements arrive in uniformly random order, and an algorithm must irrevocably accept or reject each one on arrival so as to maximize a nonnegative submodular function over sets of at most $k$ elements. For monotone objectives we settle the problem: the optimal competitive ratio tends to exactly $1-1/e$ as $k\to\infty$, and its worst case over all budgets $k$ is exactly $1/e$. The bound $1-1/e$ cannot be exceeded even with unlimited computation, and it is achieved by a single algorithm with at most $4n+1$ value queries; previously the best ratio without a shortlist was $1/e-o(1)$, with exponentially many queries. For general objectives, where the best known ratio was about $0.107$, we show that the optimal limiting ratio lies strictly between $1/e$ and $1/2$: we achieve $1/e+3.5\cdot10^{-6}$ for large $k$, and no algorithm achieves more than $0.497053$. We also achieve $0.2677$ at every budget. The main new ingredient of our algorithm is eligibility attenuation: an element that passes the price test at time $t$ is accepted with probability $e^{-τ}$, where $τ$ is the total earlier time during which it would have passed, which makes the probability that it has already been selected exactly $1-e^{-τ}$.

detail.abstract_excerpt: In just a few days’ time, U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin could be holding a three-way summit on the sidelines of next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to The Wall Street Journal, Putin floated the idea of a trialogue last month as an opportunity to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. No firm plan has yet been announced, but even the prospect of this meeting has provoked widespread consternation. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned against a repeat of the Yalta Conference of 1945, when U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill capitulated to Soviet leader Joseph Stalin’s push for the Soviet Union to dominate Eastern Europe. U.S. Senator Chris Coons posted on X that “there can be no talks about Ukraine’s future without Ukraine at the table, and there can be no real negotiations as long as Trump signals weakness and servitude to Xi and Putin at every opportunity.”

In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump announced that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”
